original_question: A first order formula φ(x) in the group language with one free variable is said to be concise in a class C of groups if for every group G in C such that the set Gφ of elements in G satisfying φ is finite, the subgroup φ(G) generated by Gφ is also finite(cf. 21.105 and Archive 2.45). Is every formula with one free variable concise in the class of residually finite groups?
target_in_paper: Problem 21.106 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)": the one-variable first-order analogue of the conciseness problem for words.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's target almost verbatim. It correctly asks about first-order formulas in the group language with one free variable, uses the right finiteness hypothesis on the set of satisfying elements, asks whether the subgroup generated by those elements must then be finite, and restricts the question to residually finite groups. It also correctly points to the nearby word-version Problem 21.105 and to Archive 2.45 as context.
missing_details: The official target is Problem 21.106, so the refined version should identify that this is the first-order analogue of the word problem in 21.105.
The notation should be made explicit: for a group G, G_φ means the set of elements g in G such that G satisfies φ(g).
The subgroup notation should be made explicit: φ(G)=⟨G_φ⟩.
To be fully stand-alone, the formula should be described as a first-order formula in the pure language of groups with exactly one free variable x.
The universal quantification should be spelled out as: for every residually finite group G, if G_φ is finite, must φ(G) be finite?
The references to 21.105 and Archive 2.45 are contextual motivation, not extra assumptions of the question itself.
refined_question: Let φ(x) be a first-order formula in the pure language of groups, with exactly one free variable x. For a group G, write G_φ={g∈G : G ⊨ φ(g)} and φ(G)=⟨G_φ⟩. Say that φ is concise in a class C of groups if, whenever G∈C and G_φ is finite, the subgroup φ(G) is also finite. Is every such one-variable first-order formula concise in the class of residually finite groups (that is, groups in which every nontrivial element has nontrivial image in some finite quotient)?
justification: The draft is essentially the exact wording of Problem 21.106, so it already identifies the right problem. The nearby context shows that 21.106 is intentionally posed as the first-order analogue of Problem 21.105 on concise words, and 21.105 explicitly points back to Archive 2.45, where P. Hall's original word-conciseness conjecture is recorded and noted as refuted in general. The paper does not give a separate equivalent reformulation of 21.106, so the sharpest paper-faithful rewrite is simply a cleaned-up stand-alone version of that yes/no question with the notation spelled out.
